Let’s dive into Chapter 4: Leading with Values and Authenticity.
Have you ever noticed how the best leaders seem to have an inner compass? That’s because values—those guiding principles we all carry—shape every decision, action, and relationship. When leaders really live out their core values, they create trust and bring a sense of steadiness, especially when things get tough or uncertain.
But how do you figure out what your core values are? Well, it starts with honest reflection. Ask yourself: What are the principles you absolutely won’t compromise on? Which qualities do you admire most in others? And maybe, what kind of legacy do you want to leave behind?
Sure, there might be a laundry list of values that matter to you. But narrowing it down to just a few central ones—that’s what brings real clarity and direction.
Once you know your values, the real test is living them out, day by day. That means making choices—big and small—that actually line up with what you believe, even if it’s hard, unpopular, or inconvenient.
It also means holding yourself, and your team, accountable to those standards. For instance, if transparency is at the heart of your leadership, you’ll share information openly, even when the news isn’t great. Or, if you deeply value respect, you’ll make sure every voice is heard, no matter someone’s position.
These little moments send a loud message about what’s important—and what simply won’t fly on your team.
But let’s be real—living your values isn’t always easy. Sometimes, it takes real courage. There’ll be moments when sticking to what you believe comes with a cost—maybe people disagree, maybe you face conflict, or maybe you have to make a tough call. Still, when you stay true, you build credibility and inspire others to do the same.
Want a practical way to lead with your values? Here are a few steps you can try:
First, get clear on your core values. Reflect, and then put them into words.
Second, check in with yourself regularly—is what you’re doing really matching up with what you say matters?
Third, talk about your values openly with your team, and explain how they guide your decisions.
Fourth, model accountability. If you slip up, own it, and show how you’re getting back on track.
And finally, invite your team to think about their own values, and encourage them to live those out, too.
Picture this: your team’s under pressure to cut corners just to hit a deadline. A leader grounded in integrity will resist that temptation, even if it means missing the mark. By explaining the “why” behind the decision—rooted in core values—you show everyone that doing the right thing always comes first.
Leading with values also creates psychological safety. When people know exactly what’s expected, and they see those expectations played out day after day, they feel more secure and engaged. There’s less guesswork, and teams can handle tough situations with confidence.
So, the big takeaway? Leading with values is really about being authentic. It’s showing up as your whole self—not just a job title—and making sure your words and actions really match. When you do that, you foster trust, resilience, and a shared sense of purpose that can pull your team through both the highs and the lows.
